results.message: Who was Jesus to your people?

voice_event.speaker: desert
voice_event.text: Three things, and the first is the one that reordered our lives. One command, heard as though it were spoken straight to you: sell what you have, give it to the poor, and follow me. Not a saying to be studied but an order to be obeyed. The second we argued for, when we were pressed to. The Word of God was not changed, but, being the same, took a human body for the salvation and well-being of man, so that having shared in human birth he might make man share in the divine nature. And we did not think this rested on our say-so: read the accounts, we told those who came to test us, and see that the deeds of Christ prove him to be God come upon earth for the salvation of men. The third is what we thought his cross had already done. The old oracles fell silent when it arose; the knowledge of God spread; and death stopped being the thing that could make a person do anything. Which is why, when persecution ended and dying for the faith was no longer offered us, we did not think we had been let off. The same fight had moved inward, against our own thoughts rather than against the sword. And the enemy we fought there was one Christ had already beaten: his coming, we said to the devil's own face, has made you weak, cast you down, and stripped you. That is why we never spoke of the healings among us as ours. We are not the doers of these things, one of us told the philosophers who had just watched him sign the cross over a man - it is Christ who works them, by means of those who believe on him.

results.message: You said following him meant obeying one command. Did anyone among you ever fail at that, and what happened to them?

voice_event.speaker: desert
voice_event.text: We do not have a story of someone who heard that command, tried to obey it, and failed - at least not one kept in the sayings or the lives we passed down. What we do have is one man's own giving taking him two hearings to complete, not one. Antony walked out of church the first time he heard it and gave away the land he had inherited, but he kept back a little for his sister's sake. Only later, hearing the same Gospel read again - do not be anxious about tomorrow - did he give away the rest as well. Even for him, in other words, the obedience was not instant and total the first time. We also know that once people had entered this life, some lived it badly - one late text among us describes monks who stayed in name only, their actions like hyenas rather than the discipline they had claimed. But that is failure inside the life, not failure at the threshold. What you are asking - whether someone heard the command, tried to follow it, could not manage it, and what became of them - we cannot answer. Our own record does not give us that story. We kept the stories of those who stayed, not the ones who turned back.

results.message: What role did women have in your tradition?

voice_event.speaker: desert
voice_event.text:
We had women among us, and some are remembered by name - Amma Sarah, Mother Talida of Antinoe, Taor, and others. Some of their own words survived, kept the same way we kept a man's saying. Sarah herself answered visiting monks who had come to humble her on the ground of her sex: by nature I am a woman, but not by my own thoughts - it is I who am the man here, and you who are the women. That was kept among us as teaching. We also remember a virgin in Alexandria, unnamed in what survives, who hid Athanasius when the Arians were hunting him - he went to her house at midnight because no one would suspect him of going to a young and beautiful woman, and she kept him safe through the whole of that time, washing his feet, seeing to what he needed, borrowing books and bringing them to him. When it was over he said he had gained two things by it, his own life and hers. The man who founded the linked houses under one rule, Pachomius, made a dwelling for his own sister across the river when she came to this life. And one voice among us said plainly that God gave women an equal measure of strength as he gave men, so that they might have no cause for being feeble in the performance of the labor of ascetic excellence.

We should tell you honestly what is missing. The named women we remember, and their reported speech, come to us in a book that narrates men the same way - third person, by the same author, at the same length. What we do not have is a woman speaking at length in her own person the way some men did. The asymmetry is not that women were only narrated while men spoke for themselves - both were narrated. voice_event.text:
Mother Talida of Antinoe, by count of what survives. The account we have says she lived sixty years in the ascetic life and never once took the key to her own dwelling out of its lock - she left it there, open to anyone, day or night, and no one ever found anything in her house worth stealing. Sixty virgins lived with her, following the same discipline. The virgin Taor, also of Antinoe, is remembered in the same telling, but more briefly. When someone offered to take her wares to market for her, she said she did not need the help, since she was not compelled to go down into the world. Melania the Great has more words attributed to her in one encounter - she identified herself by name and lineage to the governor of Palestine when he tried to use her against Rufinus, saying plainly who she was and whose wife, and that she would go to the emperor himself if necessary. But Talida's account is the longest sustained portrait of one woman's own daily practice that we kept.

We should say plainly: all three of these come to us narrated by the same outside voice, a man writing about them, not their own first-person telling. That voice narrates the men in his book the same way - third person, same length - but only for the men does our wider record also carry first-person sayings kept separately, in their own collections. What we do not have from any woman is what we have from some men: her own words, at length, in her own voice, kept as teaching on their own.

voice_event.text:
The main share in our salvation is to be ascribed not to the merit of our own works but to heavenly grace. We said that plainly, at length, and we meant it. But we did not mean it as though effort were nothing. The question was put to us directly - if a man strives with all his might for a good result, can he become master of what is good? - and the answer that started the argument was no, not unless he has it as a gift. Grace and free will look opposed to each other, but really are in harmony; we thought we ought to have both alike. We argued it from cases rather than from principles. Paul was drawn to salvation while he was eager for bloodshed, and Matthew while he was at his taking of taxes - neither was reaching for it. But Zacchaeus, and the thief on the cross, by their own desires brought violence to bear on the kingdom of heaven. Neither pattern was made to govern the other. Sometimes he puts into us the very beginnings of salvation and gives a person the zeal of his own will; sometimes he grants the carrying out of the work; and sometimes he saves people even against their will and without their knowledge, from a ruin close at hand. We took that from experience rather than from argument.

We should tell you what we do not have to give you. No letter and no story we kept speaks in so many words to whether people are born already guilty, carrying Adam's sin. On that we have no answer. What we do have is the lived tension: grace carries the main share, and the discipline we spent our lives keeping still mattered.

results.message: That sounds like it depends entirely on effort. Where does grace come into it, on your own account?

voice_event.speaker: desert
voice_event.text:
We just told you: the main share in our salvation is to be ascribed not to the merit of our own works but to heavenly grace. That is not something we are adding now to soften what we said before - it is what we argued at length, from the beginning. Sometimes he puts into us the very beginnings of salvation and gives a person the zeal of his own will; sometimes he grants the carrying out of the work; and sometimes he saves people even against their will and without their knowledge, from a ruin close at hand. We are not the doers of these things, one of us said plainly - it is Christ who works them by means of those who believe on him. Grace and free will look opposed to each other, but really are in harmony, and we thought we ought to have both alike.

If it looks to you like we depended entirely on effort, we are telling you plainly: we did not think so, and we said so ourselves, in those words. What we would not do is set grace against effort as though only one of them mattered. The beginnings, the carrying out, and sometimes the whole rescue from start to finish - all of that we ascribed to him, not to ourselves. What we also held is that the struggle still mattered, that the discipline was still ours to keep. We lived with both at once. That is the tension we carried, not a problem we solved by choosing one side over the other.
